newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB's Rich sees stable SFR despite EMU worries.
newsitem.headline: SNB's Rich sees stable SFR despite EMU worries.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) chief economist Georg Rich said the Swiss franc should remain stable for the foreseeable future despite worries about Europe's single currency project.
He also ruled out the prospect that the euro would ultimately become a parallel currency to the Swiss franc unless Swiss authorities decided they wanted this to happen.

Rich reiterated that the SNB saw no signs of inflation at present despite strong money supply growth and that it will adjust its generous monetary policy only when it sees signs of a clear upturn in the economy.

"In light of the subdued economic situation, there is no inflationary impetus from the strong growth of the money supply for the time being," Rich said, adding, "An even more expansive monetary policy would not be in line with our goal of keeping price levels stable in the medium- and long-term as well."
He also said the central bank would keep its eye on the currency.
"We will also continue to watch exchange rate developments," he said in the text of a speech he was to deliver at a seminar on the euro's impact on Switzerland.

"We probably will have to live for a long time still with the danger that broad uncertainty about the euro will lead to portfolio adjustments into the Swiss franc," Rich added, noting that current Swiss franc exchange rates should not stand in the way of economic recovery.
"The franc's exchange rate is now at a level that does not correspond with all market participants' dreams, but that should no longer seriously impede a Swiss economic recovery," he said.
He noted the SNB added extra liquidity recently to counter franc strength prompted by German plans to revalue its gold reserves and the Left's victory in French elections.
Swiss interest rates are now so low that investors seeking a safe haven must seriously question whether it is worthwhile to hold Swiss franc assets, Rich said.
The increased role of the dollar and sterling as safe haven currencies has also eased upward pressure on the franc.
"For these reasons the franc's exchange rate should remain stable for the forseeable future," he said.

Rich repeated that the SNB would continue to boost liquidity to counter renewed franc strength triggered by EMU worries and that it would consider temporarily pegging the franc to the euro in a crisis.

He also stressed the SNB's position that Switzerland wanted to retain its monetary policy autonomy and played down suggestions market forces would eventually force the Swiss to set policy in line with the EU.

"If the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank seek to fulfill their mandate to keep prices stable as well as possible, then the danger of extreme exchange rate fluctuations can be kept limited," he said.

Rich said he could imagine many Swiss companies would use the euro as the currency for invoices in contracts with foreign trading partners and that Swiss shops along the border could accept euros as payment.
But he said the euro would not eventually become a parallel currency to the franc in Switzerland.

"It can be ruled out that the euro will develop into a parallel currency in Switzerland. Swiss political authorities -- not market forces -- will decide if the franc will continue to exist independently alongside the euro," he said.

"It is up to us to determine if we want to continue to conduct our autonomous monetary policy or adjust to the euro. I see no reason why we should not continue to go our own way in the monetary field."
Rich said it was "unthinkable" that EMU would start as planned in 1999 without Germany and France, although they were having trouble getting 1997 budget deficits to the three percent of GDP ceiling.

Political pressure is strong to start on time, "but at least from today's standpoint it is not apparent how the desire for a timely transition to the third stage (of EMU) can be reconciled with the requirements in the Maastricht Treaty".
